file: papers/pdf/Denrell - 2004 - Random Walks and Sustained Competitive Advantage.pdf
about: Denrell models firm resource accumulation as a random walk and shows that pure chance can produce lasting profit differences between firms that started out identical; he argues that observers tend to wrongly credit such patterns to built-in firm superiority and build spurious explanations after the fact.

candidates.label: Superior initial resources or capabilities
candidates.definition: The conventional explanation that lasting success comes from a firm having better initial resources or a better ability to build resources (dynamic capabilities). The author sets this against chance as an explanation for the same performance record.
candidates.applies_when: The account explains a venture's sustained success by the founders or firm having better starting resources, skills or resource-building ability than others from the outset.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The account credits accumulated chance events or luck rather than differences present from the start.

candidates.label: Single lucky break sustained
candidates.definition: One lucky break can generate persistent above-average returns when it is protected by strong isolating mechanisms that keep others from imitating it.
candidates.applies_when: A participant describes one fortunate event that gave the venture an advantage, which then lasted because others could not copy or erode it.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The advantage builds up from many small chance increments rather than one break; see the code on cumulative chance.

candidates.label: Path-dependent amplification of chance
candidates.definition: In path-dependent processes with increasing returns, a firm that happens to gain an early advantage accumulates resources faster, so small chance events can lead to lasting dominance.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes an early chance advantage that made further gains easier, snowballing into a larger lead.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The lead persists without any self-reinforcement, simply because accumulated gains are retained; see the code on cumulative chance.

candidates.label: Cumulative chance producing long leads
candidates.definition: Even with no self-reinforcement, gains from many independent random draws accumulate. Once a firm happens to get ahead it is likely to stay ahead for long periods.
candidates.applies_when: A participant describes a lasting lead built from a series of chance gains that were kept, without describing any special starting advantage or self-reinforcing growth.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Gains accelerate because of the existing lead (path dependency), or the lead rests on one protected lucky break.

candidates.label: Retention and continued value of past gains
candidates.definition: Chance produces lasting differences mainly where resources gained earlier are retained and stay valuable. The effect weakens when past gains decay or lose relevance.
candidates.applies_when: An account shows that earlier fortunate gains stayed relevant and kept paying off over time.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Earlier gains became obsolete or were lost; see the code on environmental change.

candidates.label: Environmental change reversing advantage
candidates.definition: Technological or environmental change can turn accumulated resources into a liability (competency traps), so earlier leaders become laggards and chance-based leads do not last.
candidates.applies_when: A participant describes an external shift that made the venture's earlier advantages useless or harmful.

candidates.label: Attributing chance success to skill
candidates.definition: Because long streaks do not look random to people, observers and managers tend to treat persistent success as evidence of systematic superiority and to underestimate the role of chance.
candidates.applies_when: A narrator presents a sustained run of success as proof of superior strategy, ability or organization, and plays down chance.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The narrator explicitly acknowledges luck or chance as a contributor.

candidates.label: Spurious post hoc explanation
candidates.definition: There is always something special in a firm's history that can be used afterwards to explain its record, so people construct explanations for success that may in fact be due to luck.
candidates.applies_when: An interviewee builds a retrospective story linking particular features of the venture's history to its success, without evidence that those features caused it.

candidates.label: Confidence or strategy change from misread luck
candidates.definition: Misreading chance outcomes shapes later decisions: leaders grow more confident in their strategy, while laggards consider changing their strategy and organization.
candidates.applies_when: An account shows a venture reinforcing or abandoning its strategy because of a performance record that may have come from chance.
